title: The Congress Dances: Vienna, 1814–1815
subtitle: The Congress of Vienna, September 1814 – June 1815
intro: In the autumn of 1814 the victors over Napoleon gathered in Vienna to redraw the map of Europe. The Emperor of Russia and the King of Prussia rode into the city on 25 September; behind them came ministers, princes of defunct states, petitioners for cities, churches, Jewish communities and booksellers, and a crowd of hostesses, artists and spies. The Congress as a plenary assembly never met. The decisions were made in small rooms by five or so ministers, and announced in protocols drafted by a secretary.

This chapter lays those rooms beside the paper that came out of them. Talleyrand's letters to Louis XVIII are the backbone: he wrote almost daily, from the September conference where he objected to the word 'allies' to the signing of the Final Act. Around him stand Metternich, the host; Castlereagh and then Wellington for Britain; Hardenberg and Wilhelm von Humboldt for Prussia; and Tsar Alexander, who kept no diary and appears only in what others reported he said. Friedrich von Gentz, the secretary, kept a private diary whose verdicts are blunter than the minutes he wrote.

Other eyes watched from outside. Baron Hager's police agents copied embassy papers and noted who dined with whom, for Emperor Francis to read each morning. The comte de La Garde-Chambonas, a guest in the ballrooms, wrote years later the memoir that gave the Congress its reputation for dancing. Cardinal Consalvi petitioned for the Pope's lost provinces. In London, Wilberforce and the abolitionists waited for a condemnation of the slave trade; in Paris, and then in exile at Ghent, Louis XVIII read his minister's despatches.

The honest record here is mostly letters, despatches, police reports and parliamentary records, with one true diary (Gentz's) and two memoirs written later (Metternich's and La Garde's), which are flagged. Each eye wrote for a reader: Talleyrand for a king and the postal censors, Castlereagh for a cabinet and Parliament, the police for an emperor. On Poland and Saxony the positions are given as each side stated them: Russia's claim to a Polish kingdom under the Tsar, Prussia's claim to Saxony as its promised reward, and the Austrian, British and French arguments for the balance of power and for the Saxon king's legitimacy.

The slave-trade declaration of 8 February 1815 is reported for what it said and did not do: the powers condemned the trade in principle, but left each state to fix its own date and set up no enforcement. Within a month the news that Napoleon had left Elba reached Vienna (7 March); on 13 March the powers declared him outside the law. The Final Act was signed on 9 June, nine days before Waterloo.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. The Russian delegation's own papers used the Julian calendar, then twelve days behind; dates of Russian statements here are given as the Western reporters recorded them. Several printed despatch dates in the 1891 English Memoirs are garbled by OCR or misprint (e.g. a 25 vs 28 September letter); these are noted in the source notes.

eyes.name: Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord
eyes.role: French foreign minister and first plenipotentiary of Louis XVIII, aged 60; Prince of Benevento
eyes.vantage_label: the defeated power's negotiator who talked his way to the table
eyes.form: dated letters and official despatches (with a memoir narrative written later)
eyes.authenticity: The despatches to Louis XVIII and the joint despatches of the French ambassadors survive in the French foreign-ministry archives and were printed by Pallain (1881) and in the Duc de Broglie's edition of the Memoirs (1891), with English translations in both years. The connecting narrative in the Memoirs was written later and polished; Talleyrand also wrote knowing the posts were opened, so letters are part report, part performance. Dates in the printed OCR text occasionally conflict (e.g. 25 vs 28 September).
eyes.bio: Former bishop, revolutionary, Napoleon's foreign minister and then architect of the Bourbon restoration, Talleyrand arrived in Vienna representing the beaten enemy. His reports show him turning the rhetoric of 'legitimacy' and 'public law' into a lever to break the victors' exclusive circle. His letters are the fullest running account of the Congress from a single desk.

sources.title: Memoirs of the Prince de Talleyrand, ed. Duc de Broglie, English trans., vol. II (1891)
Memoirs of the Prince de Talleyrand, vol. III (1891)

eyes.name: Friedrich von Gentz
eyes.role: Austrian publicist and Metternich's adviser, aged 50; secretary of the Congress conferences
eyes.where: Vienna; the conference rooms at the Ballhausplatz
eyes.vantage_label: the secretary who kept the minutes and a private diary
eyes.authenticity: Gentz's Tagebücher were published from his papers by Varnhagen's circle (Leipzig, 1861–73). They are terse daily notes of dinners, conferences, health, money and moods, and record frankly the 'presents' he accepted from several courts. His memorandum of 12 February 1815 on the Congress survives and was printed in English in Metternich's Memoirs (1880).
eyes.bio: Born in Breslau, a translator of Burke and a fierce pamphleteer against revolutionary France, Gentz styled himself 'First Secretary of the Congress' and drafted many of its protocols. He sat in the room as recorder rather than decider, and his private verdicts are more cynical than the documents he wrote.

sources.title: Gentz, memorandum of 12 Feb 1815 (Metternich Memoirs, vol. II, doc. 192, English trans. 1880), H-Net reproduction
L.-J. Arrigon, 'Talleyrand au Congrès de Vienne' (citing Gentz's diary)

eyes.name: Klemens Wenzel, Prince von Metternich
eyes.role: Austrian foreign minister, aged 41; host and chairman of the Congress
eyes.vantage_label: the host who chaired the room
eyes.form: official notes and letters; memoir (written later)
eyes.authenticity: His notes to Hardenberg and other documents are contemporary and printed in the Memoirs (English trans. 1880). His autobiographical memoir, including the account of the night of 6–7 March 1815, was written decades later and is self-justifying; details such as times of day come only from it. His passionate letters to Wilhelmine of Sagan were published in 1966 and are not used for dated entries here.
eyes.bio: Metternich ran the Congress from his own chancery while conducting a painful affair with the Duchess of Sagan, a rival of the Tsar's favour. He wanted a Prussia strong enough to resist Russia but not so strong as to swallow Saxony, and his zigzags on that question frame the winter's crisis.

sources.title: Metternich Memoirs, vol. II, docs. 192–194 (English trans. 1880), H-Net reproduction

eyes.name: Robert Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh
eyes.role: British Foreign Secretary, aged 45; first British plenipotentiary until February 1815
eyes.where: British embassy, Minoritenplatz, Vienna; then the House of Commons
eyes.authenticity: His Vienna despatches survive in the Foreign Office papers (The National Archives) and were printed in his Correspondence (1853) and in C. K. Webster's British Diplomacy 1813–1815 (1921). His speech of 20 March 1815 is preserved in Hansard, which in 1815 was a reporter's summary rather than a verbatim transcript.
eyes.bio: Reserved and often misjudged as cold, Castlereagh came to Vienna to keep Russia out of the heart of Europe and to win an international condemnation of the slave trade that Parliament demanded. His despatches show him improvising: first backing Prussia on Saxony, then signing a secret alliance against it.

sources.title: C. K. Webster, The Congress of Vienna 1814–1815 (1919)
Hansard, HC Deb 20 March 1815

eyes.name: Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington
eyes.role: Field marshal and ambassador to France, aged 45; succeeded Castlereagh as first British plenipotentiary
eyes.where: Vienna, February–March 1815; then Brussels and Waterloo
eyes.vantage_label: the soldier sent to negotiate, recalled to fight
eyes.authenticity: His Vienna despatches are in the Wellington Papers, University of Southampton (e.g. MS 61, 1/453/7, 12 March 1815) and were printed by Gurwood in the Dispatches (1834–39).
eyes.bio: Wellington arrived in Vienna at the start of February 1815 to take Castlereagh's place and found the Saxon settlement nearly finished. Five weeks later the news from Elba turned him back into a general; he signed the declaration against Napoleon and left to command in the Netherlands.

sources.title: FutureLearn / University of Southampton: Wellington to Castlereagh, 12 March 1815

eyes.name: Karl August, Prince von Hardenberg
eyes.role: Prussian State Chancellor, aged 64 and partly deaf; first Prussian plenipotentiary
eyes.authenticity: Hardenberg kept a terse diary, published in a modern scholarly edition (ed. T. Stamm-Kuhlmann, 2000). The entries used here rest on his letters and statements as recorded in the Congress papers and in Castlereagh's despatches, which give the British reading of his words.
eyes.bio: The reforming chancellor of Prussia came to Vienna to collect the reward his king had been promised: the whole of Saxony, whose king had stayed loyal to Napoleon too long. Hard of hearing, he negotiated mostly on paper, and his position hardened as the other powers backed away.

sources.title: C. K. Webster, The Congress of Vienna (1919)
Hansard text of the declaration of 13 March 1815 (signatories)

eyes.name: Wilhelm von Humboldt
eyes.role: Prussian second plenipotentiary, aged 47; linguist and founder of Berlin University
eyes.form: official reports, signed acts and dated letters
eyes.authenticity: His letters to his wife Caroline were published in 'Wilhelm und Caroline von Humboldt in ihren Briefen' (7 vols, 1906–16); the Vienna letters (vol. IV) could not be consulted for this chapter, so entries rest on his signed acts and his official report of 15 June 1815 as cited by Webster.
eyes.bio: Brother of the explorer Alexander, Wilhelm wrote most of Prussia's memoranda at Vienna and sat on the German committee. Contemporaries found him brilliant and sardonic; his own summary of the Congress described where power had really lain.

sources.title: Wilhelm und Caroline von Humboldt in ihren Briefen, vol. V (1815–17)
C. K. Webster, The Congress of Vienna (1919)

eyes.name: Alexander I of Russia
eyes.role: Emperor of Russia, aged 36; negotiated in person
eyes.vantage_label: the sovereign who negotiated in person
eyes.authenticity: Alexander kept no diary of the Congress. What he said is known from the reports of those he spoke to (Talleyrand, Metternich, Castlereagh), each writing for his own government and with his own interest; his written memoranda to Castlereagh survive in the Foreign Office papers.
eyes.bio: Victor of 1812 and liberator of Paris, Alexander wanted the Duchy of Warsaw as a Polish kingdom under his crown and backed Prussia's claim to Saxony in return. He was the only great sovereign who negotiated face to face, which made every interview a confrontation.

sources.title: Talleyrand Memoirs vol. II–III (reports of audiences)
Webster, The Congress of Vienna (1919)

eyes.name: Franz, Baron Hager von Allentsteig (Austrian Polizeihofstelle)
eyes.role: President of the Austrian police ministry; his office compiled daily reports for Emperor Francis
eyes.where: Police headquarters, Vienna; agents in salons, embassies and servants' halls
eyes.form: police reports (agents' notes and intercepted letters)
eyes.authenticity: The reports survive in the Vienna state archives and were published selectively by August Fournier (Die Geheimpolizei auf dem Wiener Kongress, 1913) and M.-H. Weil (Les Dessous du Congrès de Vienne, 1917). They mix verified fact, servants' gossip and agents' guesses; entries here are taken as cited in Arrigon's article.
eyes.bio: Hager's agents copied papers from wastebaskets and fireplaces, bribed valets and reported who dined with whom. The reports are one-sided by design: they record what the Austrian state wanted to know, and what its informers thought it wanted to hear.

sources.title: L.-J. Arrigon, 'Talleyrand au Congrès de Vienne' (citing the police reports)

eyes.name: Auguste, comte de La Garde-Chambonas
eyes.role: French émigré man of letters, aged 31; a guest in Vienna's salons without official role
eyes.where: Vienna's ballrooms, theatres and the Prince de Ligne's house
eyes.vantage_label: the society guest outside the conference room
eyes.authenticity: His 'Souvenirs du Congrès de Vienne' were published years afterwards (1820 is uncertain; the main edition 1843) and translated into English in 1902. It is a lively but reconstructed memoir with remembered dialogue, few dates and some errors; treat details as his recollection.
eyes.bio: La Garde attached himself to the aged Prince de Ligne and recorded the Congress as a festival of balls, tableaux and carrousels. His book is the source of the most famous witticism about the Congress, and of its most moving death-bed scene.

sources.title: Anecdotal Recollections of the Congress of Vienna (London, 1902), Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: Cardinal Ercole Consalvi
eyes.role: Cardinal Secretary of State and papal envoy, aged 57
eyes.form: dated despatches to Cardinal Pacca in Rome
eyes.authenticity: Consalvi's despatches are in the Vatican archives and were used by Léon Noël in his study of Talleyrand and the papal claims; dates here follow Noël's citations.
eyes.bio: Consalvi had negotiated the 1801 Concordat with Napoleon. At Vienna he had no army and no vote, only argument, and he spent the Congress pressing to recover the Marches, the Legations, Benevento and Pontecorvo, the last two held as a title by Talleyrand himself.

sources.title: Léon Noël, 'Au Congrès de Vienne' (Consalvi and Talleyrand)

eyes.name: Louis XVIII of France
eyes.role: King of France, aged 59, restored in April 1814
eyes.where: Tuileries, Paris; from late March 1815 in exile at Ghent
eyes.vantage_label: the absent principal, reading the despatches
eyes.authenticity: His replies to Talleyrand were printed with the despatches (Pallain 1881; Broglie 1891, English translations the same years).
eyes.bio: Gouty and immobile, Louis XVIII directed Talleyrand by letter and insisted on Saxony's survival out of dynastic principle. His letters run from confidence in January to flight in March.

sources.title: Talleyrand Memoirs vol. II (1891)
Talleyrand Memoirs vol. III (1891)

eyes.name: William Wilberforce
eyes.role: MP for Yorkshire, aged 55; parliamentary leader of the abolition campaign
eyes.vantage_label: the lobby kept outside the room
eyes.authenticity: His Commons exchanges are summarised in Hansard. His diaries and letters, printed by his sons in the Life (1838), also cover 1815 but are not used for dated entries here.
eyes.bio: Abolitionist petitions with hundreds of thousands of signatures in 1814 had made the slave trade a mandate for Castlereagh at Vienna. Wilberforce watched from London, where the Vienna declaration reached him as a statement of principle without a deadline.

sources.title: Hansard, HC Deb 5 June 1815, Slave-Trade

entries.headline: The Pope's envoy arrives before the sovereigns
entries.digest: Consalvi reached Vienna weeks ahead of the crowned heads and found his fears confirmed: the territories taken from the Papal States were being treated as small change in the great bargains. He began calling on every minister who would see him.
entries.source_note: Noël, 'Au Congrès de Vienne', citing Consalvi to Pacca.

entries.date_display: 25 September 1814 (letter dated 28 September in the Memoirs)
entries.headline: First report: Russia wants Poland, Prussia wants Saxony
entries.digest: In his first letter from Vienna Talleyrand told the King he had arrived on the 24th (the Memoirs narrative says the 23rd). He had already learned the outline of the coming fight: Russia demanding Poland, Prussia ready to trade its Polish lands for German ones, and the four victors planning to settle matters among themselves through committees.
entries.source_note: Talleyrand Memoirs vol. II (1891), letter to Louis XVIII; the printed date varies between 25 and 28 September.

entries.headline: Every compensation plan points at the Legations
entries.digest: Consalvi reported to Rome that whenever the powers discussed compensating a dispossessed prince, the conversation turned to the papal Legations and to the Treaty of Tolentino that had stripped them away. The Pope's lands were the reserve fund of everyone else's settlement.
entries.source_note: Noël, citing Consalvi to Pacca, 26 Sept 1814.

entries.headline: Objecting to the word 'allies' at the table
entries.digest: Summoned with Spain's Labrador to a conference of the four powers, Talleyrand found a protocol already drafted in which the 'allied powers' would settle matters and inform France. He objected to the word, asked whether they were still at Chaumont or Laon, and against whom they were allied, since peace had been signed. The ministers withdrew the protocol.
entries.source_note: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, 4 October 1814, Memoirs vol. II (1891); joint ambassadors' despatch of the same date.

entries.headline: The secretary watches the plan collapse
entries.digest: Gentz, who was keeping the record of the conference, noted in his diary that the intervention of Talleyrand and Labrador had wrecked the ministers' arrangements and that the two had lectured them sharply. He called it a scene he would not forget.
entries.source_note: Gentz, Tagebücher, entry for 30 Sept 1814, as widely cited by historians of the Congress; wording paraphrased, not checked against the 1873 edition.

entries.date_display: an October morning 1814 (the Leipzig anniversary festival)
entries.headline: A peace festival for soldiers and sovereigns
entries.digest: La Garde described a bright, mild October morning on which the sovereigns joined a great open-air festival for the troops. He remembered it as the moment when Vienna seemed to believe war was over for good. He gives no exact day; the festival he describes matches the anniversary of Leipzig.
entries.source_note: Anecdotal Recollections (1902), ch. I, pp. 25–27; La Garde gives no date.

entries.headline: The Tsar receives Talleyrand: Poland is his
entries.digest: In a private audience the Tsar told Talleyrand that he held the Duchy of Warsaw and meant to keep it, and that the King of Prussia should have Saxony. When Talleyrand pressed the principle of legitimacy, Alexander warned that he would rather have war; Talleyrand answered with a gesture of despair rather than words, as the French report tells it.
entries.source_note: Ambassadors' despatch and Talleyrand's letter of 4 October 1814 (Memoirs vol. II); the audience's exact day is inferred.

entries.headline: Police: Talleyrand spends his evenings at Sagan's
entries.digest: An agent's report told the Emperor that Talleyrand passed his evenings at the Duchess of Sagan's, hoping to learn there what Metternich was thinking. The same note passed on gossip that Princess Bagration had found the Frenchman dull.
entries.source_note: Police report of 7 Oct 1814, cited by Arrigon.

entries.headline: Prussia asks for the whole of Saxony
entries.digest: Hardenberg put Prussia's claim in writing to Castlereagh and Metternich: assent to Prussia taking all of Saxony, together with the fortress of Mainz. Castlereagh agreed at once, on the understanding that Prussia would then stand with Austria and Britain against Russia's Polish plan.
entries.source_note: Webster, The Congress of Vienna (1919), on Hardenberg's letter of 9 Oct.

entries.headline: A memorandum to the Tsar on Poland
entries.digest: Castlereagh sent Alexander a formal memorandum and a frank covering letter arguing that a Russian-ruled Polish kingdom pushed deep into Europe would threaten Austria and Prussia. He asked how the Tsar's professed duty to the Poles could differ on either side of the line Russia proposed. The Tsar's final reply was delayed until late November.
entries.source_note: Webster (1919), on the memorandum of 12 Oct and Alexander's reply of 21 Nov.

entries.headline: Austria consents to Saxony, with conditions
entries.digest: Metternich answered Hardenberg that Austria could accept Prussia's incorporation of Saxony if no other course remained, provided Prussia joined in resisting Russia over Poland. He insisted that Bavaria, not Prussia, must have Mainz.
entries.source_note: Webster (1919); Gentz memorandum of 12 Feb 1815 (Metternich Memoirs vol. II, doc. 192).

entries.headline: A stormy audience with the Tsar
entries.digest: Metternich's interview with Alexander turned violent in tone; afterwards Metternich said he would not meet the Emperor privately again. Gentz's later summary dates the breach to this day.
entries.source_note: Gentz memorandum of 12 Feb 1815, Metternich Memoirs vol. II (English trans. 1880).

entries.headline: Agents copy French papers during a dinner
entries.digest: The police took advantage of a dinner Talleyrand gave at the Thurn und Taxis house to get at papers from the French embassy, copy them and return them before they were missed.
entries.source_note: Police report of 27 Oct 1814, cited by Arrigon.

entries.headline: No Talleyrand papers today
entries.digest: An agent reported that it had not been possible to get hold of any of Talleyrand's papers that day; only scraps from his niece's household and from a secretary had been gathered. The French had learned to burn what they threw away.
entries.source_note: Police report of 4 Nov 1814, cited (in French) by Arrigon.

entries.headline: The French niece leads a quadrille
entries.digest: Police and society observers alike noted that Dorothée, comtesse de Périgord, Talleyrand's niece and hostess, was first lady of a quadrille at the great masked ball. Talleyrand had a notice placed in the Paris Moniteur: the defeated power was dancing in the first rank.
entries.source_note: Arrigon, citing reports and the Moniteur.

entries.headline: Austria offers Prussia only part of Saxony
entries.digest: In a note to Hardenberg, Metternich withdrew the October consent and offered Prussia about 430,000 Saxon subjects instead of the whole kingdom. The Prussians took it as an insult, and talk of war grew in the Prussian camp.
entries.source_note: Metternich to Hardenberg, 10 Dec 1814, Metternich Memoirs vol. II, doc. 193.

entries.headline: The Prince de Ligne dies
entries.digest: La Garde, who had visited almost daily, described the old field marshal's last days after a chill caught seeing ladies to their carriage: erysipelas, doctors, his daughter giving him medicines, a crowd outside. Ligne joked to the end that his death would be one more spectacle for the Congress. He died on 13 December, nearly eighty.
entries.source_note: Anecdotal Recollections (1902), pp. 244–252.

entries.headline: A field marshal's funeral for the Congress
entries.digest: The funeral procession, as La Garde remembered it, had thousands of infantry, cavalry and artillery, a herald in black armour and Ligne's charger draped in black, while sovereigns watched from the old ramparts. At the burial on the Kahlenberg the sun broke through, and Gentz said it seemed to salute the favourite of God and men.
entries.source_note: Anecdotal Recollections (1902), pp. 254–256; no exact funeral date is given in the text.

entries.headline: Saxony matters more than Poland
entries.digest: Talleyrand sent the King Metternich's letter on Saxony and his own reply, his one formal note of the Congress, arguing that the survival of Saxony mattered more to the balance of Europe than the Polish frontier. Castlereagh, the joint despatch added, could not hide his embarrassment over his earlier concessions.
entries.source_note: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, No. 17, 20 Dec 1814, and ambassadors' despatch No. 20, Memoirs vol. II.

entries.headline: A heated clash over the statistics commission
entries.digest: Prussia had set up a commission to count the souls in the territories to be divided and kept France out. Talleyrand described a sharp exchange with Castlereagh and Lord Stewart and threatened to leave Vienna; France got its seat, and the Austrian emperor approved his note.
entries.source_note: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, No. 18, 28 Dec 1814; ambassadors' despatch No. 21, 27 Dec, Memoirs vol. II.

entries.headline: Prussia: refusal would mean war
entries.digest: At the conference on Saxony and Poland Hardenberg declared that denying Prussia its rights would amount to war. Castlereagh reported the words to London and drew his own conclusion: that Britain should arm a defensive combination with Austria and France.
entries.quote: tantamount to a declaration of war
entries.source_note: Castlereagh's report as quoted in Webster, The Congress of Vienna (1919).

entries.headline: Proposing a defensive treaty with France
entries.digest: Writing to Liverpool after the Prussian threat, Castlereagh explained that he had decided to propose a secret defensive alliance with Austria and France, going beyond the instruction from London to avoid war. He presented it as a way to stop war rather than start one.
entries.source_note: Castlereagh to Liverpool, 1 Jan 1815, Correspondence vol. X (1853) and Webster (1921); text not consulted directly.

entries.headline: The secret treaty is signed
entries.digest: Talleyrand announced to the King that he, Metternich and Castlereagh had signed a convention the night before: each power would put 150,000 men in the field if one was attacked. France, nine months after defeat, was inside a secret alliance against two of its conquerors.
entries.quote: the coalition is destroyed, and destroyed for ever
entries.source_note: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, No. 19, 4 Jan 1815; treaty text, Appendix I, Memoirs vol. II (1891).

entries.headline: Dinner with Metternich and Talleyrand
entries.digest: Gentz's diary notes a dinner with Metternich and Talleyrand in the week France took its seat in the directing committee. The secretary now sat with both sides of the new alignment.
entries.source_note: Gentz, Tagebücher, as cited by Arrigon.

entries.headline: A requiem for Louis XVI before the sovereigns
entries.digest: On the anniversary of Louis XVI's execution Talleyrand staged an expiatory service in St Stephen's with the sovereigns present, and asked the King for honours for the musicians and staff. The former revolutionary bishop was publicly mourning the monarch of 1793.
entries.source_note: Talleyrand's report of 21 Jan 1815, Memoirs vol. III (1891).

entries.headline: Twenty-two years after the scaffold
entries.digest: La Garde gave a chapter to the requiem, noting that twenty-two years had passed since the king's death and describing the crowded cathedral and the solemnity of the music. He recalled it as one of the Congress's grand set pieces.
entries.source_note: Anecdotal Recollections (1902), ch. XV, p. 309.

entries.headline: Wellington arrives to replace Castlereagh
entries.digest: The Duke reached Vienna to take over as first British plenipotentiary; within days the Tsar had sought him out for conversation. Talleyrand reported the arrival as 'on the 1st'; one later chronology gives 3 February.
entries.source_note: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, No. 26, 8 Feb 1815 (Memoirs vol. III); Webster's chronology (1919) reads 3 Feb.

entries.headline: The Saxon bargain is struck
entries.digest: Hardenberg and Castlereagh reached the agreement that divided Saxony: Prussia would take a large part of the kingdom, but the King of Saxony would keep his crown and Leipzig, Prussia taking Thorn and other lands in compensation.
entries.source_note: Gentz memorandum (Metternich Memoirs vol. II, doc. 192); Talleyrand's letters of 8 and 15 Feb 1815.

entries.place: Conference of the eight powers, Vienna
entries.headline: The slave-trade question 'settled' in conference
entries.digest: Talleyrand reported that the slave-trade question had been settled in a conference that day. The powers condemned the trade in principle but set no common date; Spain and Portugal would stop within eight years. Britain's long campaign won a declaration, not an enforcement mechanism.
entries.quote: Spain and Portugal will definitely cease the slave-trade in eight years
entries.source_note: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, No. 26, 8 Feb 1815, Memoirs vol. III (1891).

entries.headline: Benevento in play
entries.digest: Consalvi warned Rome of a plan to fold Benevento and Pontecorvo into the Kingdom of Naples. The enclave was Talleyrand's principality; in an earlier evening exchange Talleyrand had told the cardinal the Pope had done nothing for the common cause, and Consalvi had rebuked him.
entries.source_note: Noël, citing Consalvi to Pacca, 11 Feb 1815.

entries.headline: The secretary's verdict on the Congress
entries.digest: In a long memorandum Gentz described the Congress without its public language. The talk of rebuilding social order and lasting peace, he wrote, had been meant to calm the peoples; the real business had been the division of territory among the winners.
entries.quote: to divide amongst the conquerors the spoils taken from the vanquished
entries.source_note: Gentz memorandum of 12 Feb 1815, Metternich Memoirs vol. II, doc. 192 (English trans. 1880).

entries.headline: Castlereagh leaves for London
entries.digest: Castlereagh left Vienna for Parliament, passing through Paris to see Louis XVIII. Talleyrand recorded that Saxony would keep about 1,300,000 inhabitants and Luxembourg would go to the Prince of Orange.
entries.source_note: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, No. 27, 15 Feb 1815; Webster's chronology (1919).

entries.headline: A dispatch from Genoa at dawn
entries.digest: In his memoir Metternich recalled that, after a conference that ran into the small hours, a courier woke him early with a dispatch from the Austrian consul at Genoa: Napoleon had left Elba. He went straight to the Emperor, and by mid-morning the allied ministers had agreed to act together.
entries.source_note: Metternich, autobiographical memoir (Memoirs vol. I, English 1880); the day is confirmed by Talleyrand and Wellington, the hours rest on the memoir alone.

entries.headline: Napoleon has embarked from Elba
entries.digest: Talleyrand reported that Napoleon had sailed from Porto Ferrajo on the evening of 26 February with about 1,200 men, and blamed careless British watching. He thought a landing near Genoa unlikely and feared a march into northern Italy; he expected Austrian troops to move slowly.
entries.source_note: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, 7 March 1815, Memoirs vol. III (1891).

entries.headline: The King is 'not disquieted'
entries.digest: The same day, before Vienna's news could reach him, Louis wrote of Napoleon's 'audacious attempt' and said he had taken all the measures he thought best. He assured his ambassadors he was not disquieted.
entries.source_note: Louis XVIII to Talleyrand, No. 25, 7 March 1815, Memoirs vol. III.

entries.headline: A day trip to the captive King of Saxony
entries.digest: Wellington, Metternich and Talleyrand went to Pressburg to persuade the King of Saxony to accept the partition of his kingdom. The settlement that had nearly broken the Congress now had to be closed quickly because of the news from France.
entries.source_note: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, No. 33, 12 March 1815, Memoirs vol. III.

entries.headline: Reporting the sovereigns' resolve
entries.digest: Wellington told Castlereagh that he had heard on 7 March of Napoleon's departure with about 1,200 men and later of a landing near Cannes. The sovereigns were determined to unite to uphold the Peace of Paris and had offered their forces to the King of France; he enclosed a draft declaration and hoped the Congress would now finish quickly.
entries.quote: cordially united efforts of the sovereigns of Europe
entries.source_note: Wellington to Castlereagh, 12 March 1815, Wellington Papers MS 61 1/453/7, via FutureLearn (University of Southampton).

entries.headline: The declaration is signed
entries.digest: Talleyrand sent the declaration signed by the eight powers and ordered copies sent to every French prefect. He was proud of its force: Napoleon was put outside the law of nations.
entries.quote: I think the strength of this document leaves nothing to be desired
entries.source_note: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, No. 34, 13 March 1815, Memoirs vol. III.

entries.headline: Prussia signs the outlawing of Napoleon
entries.digest: Humboldt signed with Hardenberg for Prussia. The text declared that Napoleon had put himself outside civil and social relations and laid himself open to public vengeance, and promised the King of France the help of all the signatories.
entries.quote: without the pale of civil and social relations
entries.source_note: Declaration of 13 March 1815, English text laid before the Commons, Hansard 7 April 1815.

entries.headline: Dinner amid consternation
entries.digest: Gentz gave a dinner for Talleyrand, Metternich and the Courland sisters; at the Duchess of Sagan's supper that night he noted general consternation at the news from France, where Napoleon was advancing unopposed.
entries.source_note: Gentz, Tagebücher, as cited by Arrigon.

entries.headline: Defending Vienna to the Commons
entries.digest: Answering Whitbread's motion, Castlereagh defended the Congress: Genoa joined to Piedmont for security, a settlement on Saxony more favourable than full annexation, and Poles to be governed as Poles. On the slave trade he admitted immediate abolition had not been won. The same evening Napoleon reached Paris.
entries.quote: the Poles would now be governed as Poles
entries.source_note: Hansard, HC Deb 20 March 1815, vol. 30 cc265–305.

entries.headline: The King in flight
entries.digest: From the coast, after leaving Paris at midnight on 19 March and crossing into the Netherlands, Louis explained his departure to Talleyrand: his army had gone over to Napoleon.
entries.quote: The total defection of the troops left me no choice
entries.source_note: Louis XVIII to Talleyrand, No. 27, Ostend, 26 March 1815, Memoirs vol. III.

entries.headline: The Tsar doubts a second Bourbon restoration
entries.digest: Talleyrand reported that Alexander questioned simply restoring Louis again and floated an Orléans regency. The Tsar said overthrowing Napoleon was only half the work and that no one could rule against the ideas of the age.
entries.quote: one cannot govern in opposition to the ideas of the times
entries.source_note: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, No. 52, 23 April 1815, Memoirs vol. III.

entries.headline: Police note a departure
entries.digest: A report recorded that the comtesse de Périgord, Talleyrand's niece and hostess, had left Vienna for her family's estates. The watchers were counting the French household out of town as the Congress closed.
entries.source_note: Police report of 3 June 1815, cited by Arrigon; Noël gives the same date.

entries.headline: Asking what has been secured on the slave trade
entries.digest: Wilberforce asked whether arrangements had been made with Louis XVIII for total suppression of the slave trade if the war against Napoleon succeeded. Castlereagh said ministers would carry out Parliament's wishes; Wilberforce declared his full confidence in his noble friend.
entries.source_note: Hansard, HC Deb 5 June 1815, vol. 31 c609.

entries.headline: Signing the Final Act and leaving
entries.digest: Talleyrand signed the Final Act and left the next day for the King at Ghent. In his last weeks he had fended off a manoeuvre to delay the signature, and he left Dalberg to represent France on the remaining commissions.
entries.source_note: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, Nos. 57–58, 25 and 27 May 1815 (Memoirs vol. III); Noël on the departure of 10 June.

entries.headline: Most of the papal lands restored
entries.digest: Consalvi reported to Pacca that the Marches, the Legations, Camerino, Benevento and Pontecorvo were to return to the Pope. Avignon and a strip north of the Po were not.
entries.source_note: Noël, citing Consalvi to Pacca, 12 June 1815.

entries.headline: Where the Congress really sat
entries.digest: In his official report Humboldt described the small Committee of Five, not the assembly of states, as the real Congress. The plenary of all the powers had never met.
entries.source_note: Humboldt's report of 15 June 1815, as cited and translated in Webster (1919).

entries.headline: The battle the declaration called for
entries.digest: From Waterloo Wellington wrote his despatch to Lord Bathurst reporting the defeat of Napoleon's army the previous day with the arrival of the Prussians. The Final Act had been signed in Vienna nine days earlier.
entries.source_note: Wellington to Bathurst, 19 June 1815 (Waterloo Despatch), Gurwood, Dispatches vol. XII; not consulted directly.

entries.headline: The last Prussian leaves Vienna
entries.digest: Humboldt, who had stayed to finish the follow-up work, left Vienna for Berlin on 20 June, two days after Waterloo, before the news of the battle could have reached him.
entries.source_note: Editor's introduction, Wilhelm und Caroline von Humboldt in ihren Briefen, vol. V.

claims.claim: Objects to a protocol by which the four 'allied powers' would settle matters and inform France; protocol withdrawn
claims.evidence: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, 4 Oct 1814 (Memoirs vol. II)

claims.claim: Asks Britain and Austria to assent to Prussia annexing all of Saxony, plus Mainz
Memorandum to Alexander opposing a Russian-controlled Polish kingdom
Conditional Austrian consent to Prussia taking Saxony; Mainz to Bavaria
claims.evidence: Webster (1919); Gentz memorandum, Metternich Memoirs vol. II doc. 192

claims.claim: Offers Prussia about 430,000 Saxons instead of the whole kingdom
Declares refusal of Prussia's claims 'tantamount to a declaration of war'
Secret defensive treaty of Austria, Britain and France: 150,000 men each if one is attacked
claims.evidence: Treaty text, Appendix I, Talleyrand Memoirs vol. II; Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, 4 Jan 1815

claims.claim: France admitted to the directing committee (Committee of Five first meets 12 Jan)
claims.evidence: Webster's chronology (9 Jan); Gentz memorandum (8 Jan)

claims.claim: Agreement with Castlereagh dividing Saxony; the King keeps his crown and Leipzig
claims.evidence: Gentz memorandum, Metternich Memoirs vol. II doc. 192

claims.claim: Eight powers' declaration condemning the slave trade in principle; no common date or enforcement
claims.evidence: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, No. 26, 8 Feb 1815; Castlereagh in Commons, 20 March 1815

claims.claim: Declaration of the eight powers placing Napoleon outside civil and social relations
Whitbread's motion for papers on the Congress; Castlereagh defends the settlement
claims.evidence: Hansard, HC Deb 20 March 1815 (division not in the portion consulted)

claims.claim: Treaty of Chaumont renewed against Napoleon
claims.evidence: Talleyrand to Louis XVIII, No. 46, 29 March 1815; Webster's chronology

claims.claim: Asks whether total suppression of the slave trade has been arranged with Louis XVIII
Final Act of the Congress dated and signed (Russian signature followed later in June)
Reports that the Committee of Five had been the 'real Congress'

convergences.label: The four powers meet France and Spain
convergences.note: Talleyrand recorded a victory of principle; Gentz, writing the minutes for the hosts, recorded the same scene as the ruin of a plan. Hardenberg and Metternich are present only through their opponents' accounts.

convergences.label: The October pivot on Saxony and Poland
convergences.note: Within two weeks Prussia asked for Saxony, Britain and Austria conditionally agreed, and Metternich's audience with the Tsar broke down. Each eye records the bargain from the side that had to pay for it.

convergences.label: The death and funeral of the Prince de Ligne
convergences.note: The society memoirist made the death the Congress's emotional centre; the Gentz remark he records at the graveside is one of the few moments in which the secretary appears outside the conference room.

convergences.label: War talk and the secret treaty
convergences.note: Hardenberg's threat, Castlereagh's report of it and Talleyrand's triumphant letter form one chain: the Prussian warning produced the alliance it was meant to prevent.

convergences.label: Requiem for Louis XVI
convergences.note: Talleyrand's official report is about arrangements and honours; La Garde, writing years later, remembered the music and the crowd. Neither mentions the irony that the organiser had served the Revolution.

convergences.label: The slave-trade declaration
convergences.note: In Vienna the declaration was one item among Saxony and Naples; in London it was the measure Parliament had demanded. Castlereagh later admitted to the Commons that immediate abolition had not been won, and Wilberforce was still asking in June.

convergences.label: News from Elba
convergences.note: Metternich's later memoir makes it a dawn drama; Talleyrand's same-day letter is a cool analysis of routes and blame; Louis XVIII in Paris writes that he is not worried; ten days later Gentz notes the consternation.

convergences.label: Napoleon declared outside the law
convergences.note: One text, signed by all of them. Wellington had sent the draft to London the day before; Talleyrand had it sent to every French prefect.

convergences.label: The Final Act, Waterloo and departures
convergences.note: The Act was signed while the war it anticipated was still to be fought; Consalvi counted what the Pope had recovered, Humboldt filed his verdict, and Wellington wrote from Waterloo ten days later.

ties.note: They dined together repeatedly; Gentz's diary records the gifts he accepted from several courts, the French among them.
Allies in the secret treaty of 3 January, after a bitter clash over the statistics commission in late December.
Their early-October audience set the terms of the Polish–Saxon conflict as Talleyrand reported it.
Their audience of 24 October ended in a breach; the Tsar and the minister were also rivals at the Duchess of Sagan's.
Castlereagh first backed Prussia's Saxon claim, then reported Hardenberg's war threat and finally negotiated the partition with him on 6 February.
The two Prussian plenipotentiaries signed together; Humboldt wrote most of the papers Hardenberg presented.
The French embassy was a prime target of Hager's agents, who copied its papers and tracked its dinners.
La Garde puts Gentz at Ligne's graveside and quotes his remark about the sun.
The King and his minister exchanged letters throughout; each wrote knowing the posts might be opened.
Wellington succeeded Castlereagh at Vienna and reported to him on 12 March with the draft declaration.
Benevento was both a papal claim and Talleyrand's own principality; the two quarrelled openly over the Pope's part in the war.
Across the floor of the Commons, Wilberforce pressed and Castlereagh promised on the slave trade in June 1815.
Metternich's notes of 22 October and 10 December 1814 to Hardenberg first granted and then withdrew Saxony.

threads_out.note: On 29 November 1814 Beethoven gave a concert for the Congress in the great Redoutensaal with the Seventh Symphony, 'Wellington's Victory' and the cantata 'Der glorreiche Augenblick', before sovereigns gathered for the Congress; it marked the height of his public fame in the Vienna that would hear the Ninth ten years later.
Alexander's claim to the Duchy of Warsaw rested on the armies that had pursued Napoleon out of Russia in 1812–13; the Polish question at Vienna was the political bill for that campaign.
C. K. Webster's 'The Congress of Vienna 1814–1815', cited in this chapter, was written as a Foreign Office handbook for the British delegation to the Paris Peace Conference and published in 1919.
The Prince de Ligne was buried on the Kahlenberg, the hill from which the relief army descended on the Ottoman besiegers in 1683.
Talleyrand's requiem of 21 January 1815 marked the anniversary of Louis XVI's execution in 1793; the restored dynasty's claim to legitimacy was the principle he argued at Vienna.
